subject: Franska 4
title: Discours indirect: reported speech
sourceSummary: How to turn direct quotes into reported speech in French, including the tense shifts and changes to time and place expressions that come with it.

questions.prompt: He said: "Je suis fatigué." How does this become reported speech, introduced by "Il a dit que..."?
questions.opener: The present tense in the direct quote usually becomes the imparfait in reported speech when the main verb is in the past.
choices: Il a dit qu'il est fatigué.
Il a dit qu'il était fatigué.
Il a dit qu'il serait fatigué.
Il a dit qu'il a été fatigué.
questions.explanation: When the introducing verb ("il a dit") is in the passé composé/past, the tense in the quote shifts back one step: présent → imparfait. "Je suis fatigué" becomes "qu'il était fatigué".

questions.prompt: She said: "J'ai fini mes devoirs." How does this become reported speech? "Elle a dit que..."
questions.opener: The passé composé in the quote also shifts back one step when the main verb is in the past.
questions.explanation: The passé composé in the direct quote becomes the plus-que-parfait in reported speech after a main verb in the past: "j'ai fini" → "qu'elle avait fini ses devoirs".

questions.prompt: He said: "Je viendrai demain." How does this become reported speech? "Il a dit que..."
questions.opener: The futur simple follows the same pattern as the present and the passé composé — one step back.
questions.explanation: The futur simple in the quote becomes the conditionnel présent in reported speech after a past tense: "je viendrai" → "qu'il viendrait". Note also that the time expression "demain" (tomorrow) must change to "le lendemain" (the next day), since the reference point has shifted.

questions.prompt: She asked: "Est-ce que tu viens ?" How does the question become reported speech? "Elle a demandé..."
questions.opener: Yes/no questions with "est-ce que" are rebuilt with a special connector in reported speech.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question in reported speech is introduced by "si" (if/whether), not "que": "est-ce que tu viens ?" → "elle a demandé si tu venais". The present tense in the original question shifts back to the imparfait because "a demandé" is in the past.

questions.prompt: Il a demandé : "Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?" How does the question become reported speech?
questions.opener: "Qu'est-ce que" (what) has its own shortened form in reported speech.
choices: Il a demandé ce que je faisais ce week-end-là.
Il a demandé qu'est-ce que je faisais ce week-end.
Il a demandé quoi je faisais ce week-end-là.
Il a demandé si je faisais ce week-end-là.
questions.explanation: "Qu'est-ce que" becomes "ce que" in reported speech: "il a demandé ce que je faisais". Notice that "ce week-end" (this weekend) also changes to "ce week-end-là" (that weekend), since the perspective has moved away from the moment of speaking.

questions.prompt: Which time expression corresponds to "hier" (yesterday) when reporting a quote long after it was said?
questions.opener: Just like "demain" → "le lendemain", every time marker that points from the moment of speaking has a reported-speech equivalent.
questions.explanation: "Hier" (yesterday) becomes "la veille" (the day before) in reported speech. Common shifts: aujourd'hui → ce jour-là, demain → le lendemain, hier → la veille, maintenant → à ce moment-là, ici → là.

questions.prompt: Turn this into reported speech, starting with "Le professeur a expliqué que...": "Je corrigerai vos copies ce soir et je vous rendrai vos notes demain."
questions.opener: The sentence contains two verbs in the futur simple as well as two time expressions that both need to change.
questions.answer: Le professeur a expliqué qu'il corrigerait leurs copies ce soir-là et qu'il leur rendrait leurs notes le lendemain.
steps: The main verb "a expliqué" is in the past, so everything in the quote shifts back one tense step.
"Je corrigerai" (futur simple) → "il corrigerait" (conditionnel présent). The person also changes from "je" to "il", since the teacher is now being talked about in the third person.
"Vos copies" and "vous" (addressed to the students, in the direct quote) become "leurs copies" and "leur" when the sentence is reported to someone else.
"Ce soir" (this evening) refers to the moment of speaking and becomes "ce soir-là" (that evening) in reported speech; "demain" becomes "le lendemain".
"Je vous rendrai" (futur simple) → "il leur rendrait" (conditionnel présent), for the same reason as above.
Full sentence: "Le professeur a expliqué qu'il corrigerait leurs copies ce soir-là et qu'il leur rendrait leurs notes le lendemain."

questions.prompt: Which tense and time-expression shifts apply when turning direct speech into reported speech after a main verb in the past?
questions.opener: One step back on the tense ladder, plus swapped time and place words.
questions.answer: Tense shifts (one step back): présent → imparfait · passé composé → plus-que-parfait · futur simple → conditionnel présent · futur proche (aller + infinitive) → imparfait of aller + infinitive. Imparfait and plus-que-parfait don't change, since they're already "as far back as they go". Time/place expressions: aujourd'hui → ce jour-là · demain → le lendemain · hier → la veille · maintenant → à ce moment-là · ici → là · ce week-end → ce week-end-là. Questions: est-ce que/inversion → si · qu'est-ce que → ce que · qu'est-ce qui → ce qui. Personal pronouns (je/tu/vous) always adjust to reflect who is now talking about whom.
